message.reasoning:
I'm planning a JUnit 4 test for jsoup's Selector class, parsing HTML with Jsoup.parse to build an Element tree and verifying select() works through both Element.select() and Selector.select() directly. Since the core Jsoup classes aren't available in the given source, I need to figure out how to handle that gap.

I'm now outlining the needed imports (Jsoup, Document, Element, Elements, Selector, SelectorParseException) and drafting test cases covering null, empty, and whitespace query inputs to confirm proper exception handling.

I also want to check null root handling, the combinator branch when selectors like "div p" recurse internally, and all the different findElements paths — id, class, tag, attribute, wildcard, index-based pseudo-selectors (:lt, :gt, :eq), :has, and :contains.

I should cover text-matching pseudo-selectors like :containsOwn and regex-based :matches/:matchesOwn, malformed tokens throwing SelectorParseException, grouped selectors with commas, all combinator types, namespace tags, the various attribute operators, attribute presence checks, non-numeric index validation errors, and selecting across multiple/empty/null root collections. Now I need to construct the actual HTML test fixtures to exercise these cases.

I'm sketching a sample document with nested divs, classes, and spans, then building a more complete test HTML with ids, multiple classes, and data attributes to verify basic selectors like byId work correctly, including the case where no match is found.

Next I'm planning tests for class and tag selectors, namespaced tags, and various attribute matchers -- presence, prefix, equals, not-equals, starts-with, and ends-with -- to make sure each selector variant correctly filters elements by their attributes.

I'm also outlining tests for "contains" and regex attribute matching, the universal "*" selector, index-based pseudo-selectors like :lt, :gt, :eq, error handling for invalid index arguments, and structural/text selectors like :has, :contains, :containsOwn, and :matches.

I need to add actual digits to the test text for :matches to work properly. I also need a test confirming that an unrecognized token like "&" throws a SelectorParseException, since none of the parser branches handle it, plus a test for grouped selectors like "div, p".

Next I want to cover combinator tests: child (">"), adjacent sibling ("+"), general sibling ("~"), and descendant (space). I'm also considering whether a query starting with a combinator is reachable through the public API, since the Selector constructor is private and only accessible via select(query, root), so testing that branch directly may not be straightforward.

I should also test leading whitespace before a combinator, confirming it gets trimmed and matched correctly. The unreachable "unknown combinator" exception path isn't testable through public API, so I'll skip that. For the roots-based select overload, I need tests covering empty query, null query, null roots, and empty roots collection, since Validate.notNull on roots only checks for null, not emptiness.

Now I'm moving to the actual JUnit test implementation, setting up imports for Jsoup, Elements, Selector exceptions, and JUnit annotations, then building a setUp method with a Document containing namespaced tags, data attributes, and numeric text for match testing.

The byTag selector replaces "|" with ":" to match namespaced tags, so "fb|name" in a selector maps to the literal "fb:name" tag in HTML—this matches jsoup's own test patterns for namespace selectors. I'll trust this behavior and construct the test HTML accordingly.

Now I need to think through sibling indices carefully for :lt, :gt, :eq tests, since these are based on position among all sibling elements regardless of tag type, not just matches within the same tag—so within div#1 the children p.one, p.two, span, and fb:name occupy sibling indices 0 through 3 respectively.

Continuing the trace: after consuming "p", no whitespace follows so it falls into the implicit-AND branch, where findElements() parses ":lt(2)" as an index-based filter pulling all elements with sibling index under 2 regardless of tag, then intersects that candidate set with the previously matched "p" elements to get the final result.

Checking sibling indices within each parent: div#1 has p.one at 0, p.two at 1, span at 2, fb:name at 3; div#2 has p-Three at 0 since it's an only child. So "p:lt(2)" ends up matching all three paragraphs since each has an index under 2, which seems like an odd result worth double-checking.

Testing other selectors: "p:eq(0)" catches p.one and p-Three (two matches), "p:gt(0)" catches only p.two (one match), and "p:eq(1)" also catches just p.two. These give cleaner distinguishing results. For the :has case, "div:has(span)" only matches div#1 since div#2 lacks a span descendant.

For text-based filters, "p:contains(jsoup)" and "p:containsOwn(jsoup)" both pick up p.two ("Two jsoup") since there's no nested markup to differ own-text from full text, and similarly ":matches(\\d+)" and ":matchesOwn(\\d+)" both match p-Three ("Three 123") for the same reason.

Moving to attribute selectors now: "[data-test]", "[^data-]", and "[data-test=1]" all converge on matching the span element, since it's the only one carrying that data attribute with value "1".

For "[data-test!=2]" though, I need to think through jsoup's actual behavior - this uses a "not equal" match which typically returns elements that don't have that exact value, including elements that lack the attribute entirely (since a missing attribute defaults to empty string, which isn't "2"). That means this selector could end up matching nearly every element in the tree since none of them have data-test=2.

Rather than asserting a precise count, which depends on knowing the full tree size, I think it's more reliable to just verify the result isn't empty and includes the span element, grabbing that span via a simple select call for setup purposes.

Trying "div[id!=2]" to test the not-equals branch gets tricky though—it would also match html/body elements whose missing id attribute defaults to "" which is != "2", so the match set is broader than intended unless the selector parsing scopes attribute matching to the preceding tag token properly.

The intersection then narrows that broad candidate set down against the current "div" results, leaving only div#1 since div#2's id equals "2" and gets excluded. Testing "[id^=1]" alone should similarly isolate div#1 as the sole element whose id starts with "1".

I keep working through each attribute selector variant—suffix match, substring match, and regex-based matching—tallying expected match counts for div1 and div2 based on their ids "1" and "2". Now I want to verify the universal "*" selector returns the full document element count, which should be ten total nodes.

I'm thinking it's safer to compare against the actual `doc.getAllElements()` result rather than hardcoding a number, since miscounting elements is easy. I also want to add a test confirming that an unrecognized token like "&" triggers a SelectorParseException, since it doesn't match any valid selector pattern (id, class, tag, attribute, wildcard, or pseudo-selector).

For a group selector like "div, p", I expect it to match all divs and paragraphs combined, so I'll verify the total count equals five without duplicates. Then for the child combinator "div > p", I'm working out that all three paragraph elements qualify since each is a direct child of its parent div.

To actually distinguish child from descendant selectors, I realize I need deeper nesting in my test HTML, so I'm restructuring it: div#2 will now contain both a direct paragraph and a nested div#3 that itself wraps another paragraph labeled "Deep," letting me verify "div p" catches the deeper one while "div > p" doesn't.

So select on "p" under the combined div roots gathers all descendant p's across the three divs, then filterForChildren narrows that candidate set to only those whose immediate parent is one of the divs - meaning p.one and p.two qualify since div1 is their direct parent, and p-Three qualifies since div2 is its direct parent, but p-deep is excluded since its direct parent is div3's descendant, not a div itself at the top level.

Wait, actually I realize p-deep's parent might literally be div3 if div3 itself was one of the matched elements, which would wrongly include it - to avoid that ambiguity I should restructure the test fixture so p sits inside a span inside div2, making the child vs descendant distinction unambiguous.

Redesigning the HTML: div1 keeps p.one, p.two, a span, and fb:name; div2 gets p-Three as a direct child plus a span.wrap containing p.deep nested one level deeper. That way "div p" (descendant) picks up all four paragraphs, while "div > p" (direct child) only picks up p.one, p.two, and p-Three, correctly excluding p.deep.

Now I'm assembling the final markup and working out sibling indices within each div for the :lt/:gt/:eq tests — div1's children order is p.one, p.two, span, fb:name, while div2's direct children are p-Three then span.wrap, with p.deep sitting at index 0 inside span.wrap itself.

So checking "p:lt(1)" across the whole doc, since elementSiblingIndex is relative to each element's own parent, p.one(0), p-Three(0), and p.deep(0) all qualify while p.two(1) doesn't.

For "p:gt(0)" only p.two(1) matches, giving 1 result, and "p:eq(0)" matches the same three as lt(1). I'll use eq(1) to isolate p.two for a single-match eq test, and gt(0) also gives that same single match.

Now checking sibling selectors: "p + span" matches spans immediately following a p sibling, which happens for both spans across div1 and div2, giving 2 matches. The general sibling "~" selector gives the same 2 matches here since there's only one preceding p in each case, so I need a case where they'd differ to distinguish them.

To differentiate, fb:name is a good test case: its immediate previous sibling is span, not p, so "p + fb|name" should return zero matches, while "p ~ fb|name" should still match since p.one and p.two appear earlier among its siblings even though not immediately before it.

For the general sibling filter logic, I'm confirming it just checks same parent and that the candidate's sibling index is greater than the earlier element's index, without requiring adjacency.

For the "+" (immediate sibling) test case, I trace through: with only one fb:name candidate, I check its previous element sibling against each p.one/p.two in the same parent div, and since the immediate previous sibling is a span rather than a p, this should fail to match, confirming the stricter adjacency requirement of "+" versus "~".

Now verifying "p + span": for the span under div1, its immediate previous sibling is p.two, so that pairing should match correctly.

For span.wrap under div2, only p-Three qualifies as a matching sibling since p.deep's parent is actually span.wrap, excluding it. The previous sibling check confirms p-Three matches, giving two total matches as expected.

Next I want to verify the ":has(span)" selector by tracing how it filters elements for those containing descendant spans.

So the result is {div1, div2} since both divs contain spans, which isn't very distinguishing. Instead I'll test with "div:has(span.wrap)" to isolate div2 alone, or alternatively "div:has(fb|name)" which should match only div1 since that's the only one containing the fb:name namespaced tag - this also checks that subquery parsing handles namespace pipes correctly inside the parentheses.

Let me also verify "div:has(span.wrap)" works correctly: parsing "span.wrap" as tag+class filters down to just the span.wrap element, then checking which divs have that as a descendant should match only div2.

Next I want to test ":contains" - checking that "p:contains(jsoup)" correctly finds elements with case-insensitive text matches anywhere in the document, searching both self and descendant text content.

So the candidates matching "jsoup" would include html, body, div1, and p.two, but intersecting with the current "p" elements leaves only p.two, matching the expected single result. For containsOwn, since it checks only an element's own text excluding descendants, only p.two itself qualifies, giving the same result of one match.

For the matches test checking digits via regex, p-Three's text "Three 123" contains digits, and while ancestor elements also technically contain digits in aggregated text, intersecting with the p set narrows it down to just p-Three, again one match.

I'm also planning tests for byId lookups that return empty when not found, plus checking consistency between the select API and Element.getElementById. Then I want to trigger the exception branch in byAttribute for unrecognized operators like "?=" -- I need to figure out exactly when cq ends up non-empty but matches none of the known delimiters so the else branch actually throws.

This turns out to be practically unreachable through normal input since consumeToAny always stops right at a known token or empties out, so I'll skip that branch with a comment explaining why. Similarly, the "Unknown combinator" IllegalStateException is unreachable via the public API since the combinator set is fixed, so I'll skip it with a note too, along with the byAttribute "unexpected token" else branch. Now I'm turning to testing SelectorParseException itself, checking that constructing it with a formatted message and argument produces the expected message string.

Then I need to write the actual test setup with @Before creating a Document, and add tests for the select(String query, Iterable<Element> roots) overload directly rather than through Element.select. I want to cover selecting across multiple root elements (checking duplicates get merged via LinkedHashSet), an empty roots list returning an empty result, and a null roots argument throwing some exception -- though I'm unsure whether Validate.notNull throws IllegalArgumentException or NullPointerException since I don't have its implementation.

Since the exact type is uncertain, I'll use `@Test(expected = RuntimeException.class)` which will pass as long as any RuntimeException subtype is thrown, avoiding the need to guess the precise exception class.

Similarly, for Selector.select with null query, null root, or empty query, the validation order (notNull on query, trim, notEmpty, then notNull on root) determines which check fails first, so I'll craft tests around that sequence and expect RuntimeException in each case. I also want to add a case-insensitivity test, like querying "DIV" uppercase to confirm it still matches lowercase div tags per the documented behavior.

I'm now drafting the final list of test method names covering null query, empty query, whitespace query, null root, combinator-starting query, and ID lookup success/failure cases.

Extending the list to cover class, tag, namespace, attribute variants (prefix, equals, not-equals, starts-with, ends-with, contains, regex), index comparisons, consume-index errors, has/contains/matches checks, unhandled token errors, group selectors, and combinators — rounding out roughly thirty distinct test cases.

Now listing the remaining combinator tests (descendant, adjacent sibling, general sibling, mismatched sibling cases), plus select-iterable-roots edge cases for multiple roots, empty lists, null throws, empty query throws, and a selector parse exception message format check.

I'm planning the test implementations now, making sure to reference real jsoup Element API methods like getElementById, select, parents, elementSiblingIndex, and previousElementSibling so everything compiles correctly against the actual classpath.

I should also include a Thai summary table mapping test methods to branches, and add comments flagging branches like "Unknown combinator" and "unexpected token" inside byAttribute that aren't testable through the public API, per the rule against guessing unverified behavior.

I'm checking whether "fb|name" conversion to "fb:name" works properly, trusting that Jsoup's HTML parser handles colon-containing tag names as normal unknown tags, similar to patterns used in jsoup's own test suite -- though I'm wary of edge cases with self-closing custom tags being auto-closed unexpectedly.

Now I'm assembling the full HTML test fixture, using single quotes for attributes inside the Java string to avoid escaping issues, structuring nested divs, paragraphs, and spans with specific classes and ids to match the selector test cases.

With the fixture built, I plan the JUnit test methods to use Selector.select against the Document directly, covering attribute selectors like `[id!=2]`, `[id^=1]`, `[id$=1]`, `[id*=1]`, and `[id~=\d]` as individual test cases.

Writing the final Java test class now, including a dynamic assertion comparing against doc.getAllElements().size() rather than hardcoded counts. I also want to add a direct test for SelectorParseException's formatted message, confirming it extends IllegalStateException and verifying the unhandled-token case with a proper root element.

For invalid numeric input like ":lt(abc)", I'm uncertain whether Validate.isTrue throws IllegalArgumentException or something else since that class isn't shown, so I'll lean toward a safe RuntimeException superclass expectation for that test case.

I'll annotate this uncertainty in comments as requested, then put together the final write-up in Thai with a summary table mapping each test to its branch/condition.
